analysis.one_liner: Forces approval of pending federal coal leases and lifts the federal coal leasing moratorium.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late October 2025 by Wyoming's two Republican senators with a single cosponsor, the bill has sat in the Senate Energy Committee with no action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill orders the Interior Department to finish and approve every pending application to lease federally owned coal, including publishing the required environmental assessment and setting the fair market value of each tract. It also orders extra approvals needed so mining can start on coal leases already awarded. Finally, it wipes out a 2016 Obama-era order that put most new federal coal leasing on hold pending a program-wide review.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal companies with applications pending to lease coal on federal land, which would be guaranteed approval rather than left to the agency's judgment. Coal miners and coal-dependent communities could see new or continued mining work. Coal-fired power plants gain a steady pipeline of federal coal supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal companies with pending federal lease applications

how_it_helps.text: The Bureau of Land Management must publish a draft environmental assessment, finalize the fair market value of each tract, take every intermediate step, and grant each pending coal lease application whose environmental review has already begun.
For coal leases already awarded, Interior must grant any additional approvals its agencies require before mining can commence.
The bill nullifies Secretarial Order 3338, the 2016 hold Interior placed on most new federal coal leases until a comprehensive review of the federal coal program was complete.

analysis.who_pays: The public, which owns the coal under federal land. Environmental review would still occur, but the outcome would be fixed in advance: the agency must approve each lease no matter what its assessment finds. Broader costs fall on people affected by mining and by the emissions from burning the coal, while other energy producers compete against mandated federal coal supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public that owns federal coal minerals

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the agency to publish a draft environmental assessment but then to grant the lease regardless, making the review a formality rather than a real evaluation of a mining project's effects.

Nullifying Secretarial Order 3338 removes the pause that let the government study the entire federal coal program — its pricing, its environmental effects, and its return to taxpayers — before committing more public coal to the market.

Mandating new federal coal leasing sustains coal-burning generation and its air pollution and climate emissions at a time when other sources are increasingly cost-competitive, a cost an honest supporter of coal jobs would have to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but concentrated: guaranteed leases for companies with pending applications and employment in coal regions. The costs are diffuse and borne by everyone — mining's local impacts, emissions from the coal burned, and an environmental process whose conclusion is predetermined. The bill is designed so that the review happens but cannot change the result, which undermines the reason such reviews exist.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in October 2025 and has had no further action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Cynthia Lummis introduced S. 3045, the COAL Act of 2025, on October 23, 2025, for herself and Sen. John Barrasso.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day, and no markup, hearing, or vote has followed.
One Republican senator has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost: the federal coal moratorium remains on the books and no lease has been mandated or blocked, because the bill has not moved past committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Cynthia Lummis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring Interior to grant pending federal coal lease applications and to nullify the federal coal leasing moratorium.

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred yet; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on, so any future split would likely follow party lines, though the record so far shows no opposition activity.

industries.note: The bill converts pending federal coal lease applications into mandatory approvals and reopens federal coal leasing generally, giving companies guaranteed access to coal owned by the public. Coal-mining jobs are real working-class employment in places like Wyoming, so some of the gain reaches ordinary workers, while the environmental costs of mining and burning the coal fall on the broader public.

A mandated pipeline of new federal coal leases supports long-term fuel supply for plants that burn coal. Cheaper fuel can pass through to ratepayers, but continued coal generation carries pollution and climate costs the bill does not address.

Mandated federal coal leasing keeps coal supplied to the market regardless of demand shifts, sustaining competition against wind, solar, and storage projects that would otherwise displace it. Some renewable development also brings jobs to the same energy-producing regions.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and no committee action in the weeks since referral, the bill follows the path of most Senate bills: it is likely to die in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee unless its sponsors push for a hearing or the committee schedules a markup before the Congress ends in January 2027.
